The Big Three Cloud AI Platforms

Every major cloud offers an end-to-end machine-learning platform: Azure Machine Learning, Amazon SageMaker, and Google Vertex AI. Each provides managed compute, notebooks, training jobs, model registries, and one-click deployment endpoints so teams can focus on models instead of servers.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Renting cloud AI is like renting a fully equipped kitchen instead of building one. You bring the recipe (your data and model); the provider supplies the ovens (GPUs), plumbing (networking), and cleanup (patching).

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

You submit a training job referencing a dataset and a compute cluster. The platform provisions GPU/CPU nodes, runs your container, logs metrics, saves the model artifact, then tears the cluster down. Deployment wraps the model in a REST endpoint that autoscales with traffic.

📝 KEY IDEA

Cloud AI is pay-as-you-go: you are billed for compute-seconds and storage, not a flat license. Idle GPUs still cost money, so shut clusters down.

  • Azure ML — deep Microsoft/enterprise integration, designer UI, and pipelines.
  • SageMaker — the broadest toolset on AWS: Studio, built-in algorithms, and endpoints.
  • Vertex AI — unifies Google's AutoML and custom training with strong BigQuery ties.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Under the shared-responsibility model the provider secures the infrastructure, but YOU remain responsible for your data, access controls, and model outputs. The cloud does not automatically make you compliant.

"},"AIM-INFRA/ch1/s2":{"body":"

Managed Services and Proving Your Skills

Beyond raw compute, clouds sell managed AI services at three levels: pre-built AI APIs (vision, speech, language), AutoML that trains custom models with little code, and fully managed custom training. Higher levels trade control for speed.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Pre-built APIs are like buying a ready meal, AutoML is a meal-kit, and custom training is cooking from scratch. All feed you; they differ in effort and flexibility.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

With AutoML you upload a labeled dataset and pick a task type. The service searches architectures and hyperparameters automatically, then returns a deployable model plus evaluation metrics, no manual training loop required.

📝 KEY IDEA

Vendor certifications signal role-ready skills. Key ones: Azure AI Engineer (AI-102), Azure Data Scientist (DP-100), AWS Certified Machine Learning – Specialty, and Google Professional Machine Learning Engineer.

CertFocus
AI-102Building AI apps with Azure Cognitive/AI services
DP-100Data science and ML on Azure ML
AWS ML SpecialtyML modeling and ops on AWS
Google PMLEDesigning ML solutions on Google Cloud
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Do not reach for custom training when a pre-built API already solves the task. Rebuilding sentiment analysis from scratch wastes weeks that a language API solves in an hour.

"},"AIM-INFRA/ch2/s1":{"body":"

Packaging and Running Models Anywhere

Docker packages your code, dependencies, and runtime into a portable image. A running instance of that image is a container. This solves 'it works on my machine' by shipping the whole environment.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An image is a recipe frozen in a box; a container is the meal you actually cook from it. One box can produce many identical meals on any kitchen.

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "serve.py"]
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each Dockerfile instruction adds a cached layer. Reordering so rarely-changed steps (installing dependencies) come before frequently-changed steps (copying code) speeds up rebuilds because unchanged layers are reused.

📝 KEY IDEA

Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many machines. The smallest deployable unit is a pod (one or more containers). A Deployment keeps a desired number of pod replicas running and self-heals.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Containers are ephemeral. Writing important data to a container's local filesystem loses it on restart, use external volumes or object storage for state.

"},"AIM-INFRA/ch2/s2":{"body":"

Remembering Every Experiment

Training dozens of model variants without records is chaos. MLflow Tracking logs each run: its parameters, metrics, and output artifacts, so results are reproducible and comparable.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

MLflow is a lab notebook that writes itself. Every experiment's settings and scores are stamped and filed so you can always find your best result later.

import mlflow
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("n_estimators", 200)
    mlflow.log_metric("f1", 0.91)
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, "model")
⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each run stores params (inputs you set), metrics (numbers you measure), and artifacts (files like the model or plots). A tracking server backs this with a database and artifact store you can query from the UI.

📝 KEY IDEA

The Model Registry versions models and moves them through stages such as Staging and Production, giving a governed path from experiment to deployment.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Logging metrics but not the exact parameters, data version, and code commit breaks reproducibility, you may never recreate that 'great' run.

"},"AIM-INFRA/ch2/s3":{"body":"

Automating the Path to Production

CI/CD means Continuous Integration (automatically test and merge changes) and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (automatically ship them). For ML this expands to also test data and models, not just code, a practice sometimes called CI/CD/CT (continuous training).

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A pipeline is an assembly line: raw data enters one end, and a validated, deployed model rolls out the other, with quality checks bolted along the way.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A typical ML pipeline chains stages: ingest → validate data → transform/feature-engineer → train → evaluate → register → deploy. A failing gate (e.g. accuracy below threshold) stops promotion automatically.

stages:
  - ingest
  - validate_data
  - train
  - evaluate   # gate: f1 >= 0.90
  - deploy
📝 KEY IDEA

A feature pipeline computes reusable features (often into a feature store) so training and serving use identical logic, preventing training-serving skew.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Testing only code, not data quality or model metrics, lets a perfectly 'green' build deploy a model degraded by bad input data.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

Watching Models After Launch

A model's accuracy is highest the day it ships and can decay as the world changes. Model monitoring tracks live inputs, predictions, and outcomes to catch that decay before it hurts users.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A deployed model is like milk with an invisible expiry date. Monitoring is the sniff test that warns you it has gone off, so you can retrain before customers taste it.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Monitoring compares the live input distribution against the training baseline. Statistics like Population Stability Index or KS tests flag when incoming features shift far enough to trigger an alert or retraining.

📝 KEY IDEA

Data drift is a change in the input distribution (P(X)). Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target (P(Y|X)), the rules themselves change.

  • Data drift example: a new user demographic sends different-looking inputs.
  • Concept drift example: fraud tactics evolve, so the same features now imply a different label.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Watching only system metrics (latency, uptime) misses silent model rot. A fast endpoint can still return increasingly wrong predictions.

📊 FIGURE — monitoring before the labels arrive
🎯 EXAM TIP
Measuring live prediction accuracy directly requires eventual ground-truth labels — until the true outcome arrives there is nothing to compare against. That label lag is why production monitoring leans on proxies you can see immediately: feature drift, prediction distribution, and confidence.

Throughput, Latency & Little's Law

Little's Law relates concurrency to arrival rate and residence time: an offered rate of requests spends time in the system, and their product is the average number in flight. Provisioning must cover peak arrival divided by target utilization, never mean load.

⚙️ FORMULAS
  • L = λ · W (in-flight = arrival rate × latency)
  • Replicas = ceil( (λ / util_target) / per_replica_capacity )
  • Training mem/param (fp16 + Adam) = 2 (weights) + 2 (grads) + 12 (fp32 master + m + v) = 16 bytes
  • Amdahl speedup = 1 / ( (1−p) + p/N ); scaling efficiency = speedup / N
  • Cost/1k = ($/hr) / 3600 / (inf/s) · 1000
  • Series availability = ∏ Aᵢ; downtime = (1−A) · period
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • A 7B model in mixed-precision Adam needs ~112 GB of optimizer/gradient/weight state alone.
  • 99.9% ("three nines") ≈ 43.2 min downtime per 30-day month.
  • Two 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.8% end-to-end.
📝 TECHNIQUE

Global batch = micro-batch × grad-accum-steps × data-parallel-world-size. Inference KV cache and activations dominate memory at long context; training is dominated by optimizer states.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Sizing replicas at 100% utilization guarantees queue blow-up — Little's Law shows unbounded W as ρ→1. Always divide by a target utilization (e.g., 0.7). Linear scaling is a fiction: communication (all-reduce) grows the serial fraction, capping speedup well below N.

📊 FIGURE — two numbers to be able to produce
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The error budget, and the ceiling on parallelism

SLA. A 30-day month is 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. A 99.9% availability target permits 0.1% of that:

0.001 × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes

Each additional nine divides by ten: 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes, 99.999% about 26 seconds. That is the whole "how many nines" conversation in one line.

Amdahl. With 95% of the work parallelisable, speedup = 1/((1 − 0.95) + 0.95/N). As N grows the second term vanishes:

speedup → 1/(1 − 0.95) = 1/0.05 = 20×

Concretely: 10 workers give 6.9×, 100 give 16.8×, 1000 give 19.6× — and infinite workers still give only 20×. The 5% serial fraction caps everything, which is why removing serial bottlenecks matters more than adding machines.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Two computations worth being able to do cold. A 99.9% SLA over 30 days allows 43.2 minutes of downtime (0.001 × 43,200). And Amdahl's asymptotic speedup for a 95%-parallel job is 20× — 1/(1−p) — no matter how many workers you add.

Drift Statistics, Rollouts & Correctness

Drift monitors compare a production distribution against a reference (training) distribution. PSI and the KS statistic are the workhorses; both bin or rank data and quantify divergence, with fixed action thresholds.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
⚙️ FORMULAS
  • PSI = Σ (aᵢ − eᵢ) · ln(aᵢ / eᵢ) over bins (a = actual %, e = expected %)
  • KS statistic = max |F_ref(x) − F_prod(x)|
  • KS critical (α=0.05) = 1.36 · sqrt((n+m)/(n·m))
  • Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN)
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • PSI < 0.1 = stable; 0.1–0.25 = moderate shift (investigate); > 0.25 = significant shift (act).
  • KS rejects "same distribution" when the statistic exceeds the critical value.
📝 TECHNIQUE

Shadow deployment mirrors live traffic to a new model with no user impact — pure correctness/latency comparison. Canary routes a small real-traffic slice and needs enough samples for a statistically valid error-rate comparison before ramping.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Training-serving skew comes from different code paths computing the same feature offline vs online; identical model + identical inputs must give identical outputs. CT (continuous training) that auto-promotes without a validation gate re-learns drift into the model. Reproducibility requires pinning data snapshot, code, seed, and environment — not just the model artifact.

"},"AIM-INFRA/aistote/s1":{"body":"

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
